title: Profile
text:
Hi, I’m Hui Ying!
I am a Research Fellow at Singapore Management University (SMU) and a Visiting Scholar at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). My research sits at the confluence of water systems, climate risk, environmental governance, and the translation of evidence into practical decisions.
My work spans water-quality measurement, remote sensing, physical and statistical modelling, and climate-risk assessment. I work across the full chain from field and sensor data to interpretable risk frameworks and policy-relevant insights, with a particular focus on cascading and compounding risks in Asian cities.

current research
At SMU, I develop climate-risk assessments for Singapore using downscaled climate projections, probabilistic pluvial-flood models, and mobility and productivity simulations. These assessments are being operationalised through a VR platform as a communication tool to improve the translation of climate projections into policy. With Cooling Singapore 2.0, I lead the development of a Heat Risk Index for Singapore while engaging government stakeholders to identify policy salience and translate research insights into actionable policies for urban heat planning.
At MIT, through the Center for Real Estate and the Department of Urban Studies and Planning, my work focuses on climate risk, sustainable cities, and real-estate responses in Singapore, including the effects of pluvial floods and adaptive infrastructure on housing markets. I am currently exploring research on the environmental governance of data centres and AI infrastructure, particularly cross-border data-centre arrangements between Singapore and Malaysia.
Earlier research at Nanyang Technological University connected environmental monitoring, remote sensing, and machine learning across riverine, inland-water, and coastal environments in Malaysia and Singapore. I also develop open-source projects and share my research output for use beyond academia.

title: Pak Hui Ying
text:
Singapore | (+65) 9272 5582 | pakhuiying@gmail.com | Website | GitHub


Geospatial and environmental data researcher with 8+ years of experience applying GIS, remote sensing, spatial analysis, Python and machine learning to complex environmental, climate-risk and urban datasets. Experienced in designing reproducible spatial workflows, validating and geocoding multi-source data, developing automated processing tools, and communicating spatial insights to technical and non-technical stakeholders. Brings strong experience translating geospatial evidence into decision-support outputs for government and operational users.




GIS and spatial analysis: QGIS, ArcGIS Pro, geospatial data processing, spatial matching, georegistration, spatial databases and cartographic visualisation
Programming, automation and version control: Python (geopandas, shapely, osgeo, GDAL, rasterio, netCDF and OSMnx), R/RStudio, MATLAB and Git/GitHub
Data wrangling, analysis and machine learning: numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn and PyMC
Geospatial data formats: GeoParquet, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GeoTIFF/TIFF and NetCDF
Spatial databases: SQLite, Firebase and DuckDB (currently exploring)
Remote sensing: UAV multispectral and hyperspectral imagery, image correction, sun-glint correction, image alignment, turbidity mapping and Google Earth Engine (GEE)
Data quality and integration: multi-source data collection, geocoding, data-owner validation, spatial data quality checks, environmental and built-environment datasets
Analytics and visualisation: machine learning, Bayesian modelling, statistical analysis, GeoLibre, Leaflet and scientific figures

Conducted research on climate risk, sustainable cities and real estate in Asia, including pluvial-flood impacts, adaptive infrastructure and housing-market responses.
Applied econometric and spatial methods to connect flood records, drainage projects, housing transactions and urban-policy questions, and supported research on the resilience of Asian cities’ urban growth amid supply-chain shocks and geopolitical tensions by establishing interviews with government agencies and industry stakeholders in Southeast Asia.





Led Singapore climate-risk assessments using downscaled climate projections, socio-economic and demographic data, health outcomes, built-environment data, transport networks and other spatial datasets.
Developed probabilistic pluvial-flood risk models and conducted vehicle-routing simulations to estimate productivity loss as travel-time delays from flood-affected roads for private and public transport modes under three extreme pluvial-flood scenarios: historical, operational and future extremes.
Developed a Singapore Heat Risk Index through Cooling Singapore 2.0 by calculating service areas and walking distances via pedestrian-path networks to MRT station exits and bus stops to estimate exposure to heat during transit.
Collected, integrated and geocoded flood locations, hydrographic data, drainage infrastructure, private housing, road networks, meteorological weather-station data, transport data and other built-environment datasets from data.gov.sg for spatial analysis.
Demonstrated proficiency using the LTA DataMall API and OneMap API to automate extraction of relevant transport and geospatial datasets for research applications.
Engaged government agencies and stakeholders, including LTA, to obtain feedback on the relevance of the Heat Risk Index for informing policy and to refine approaches for estimating exposure to heat during transit.
Operationalised complex climate-risk findings through a virtual-reality platform that communicated projections and supported policy exploration.





Developed a Water Quality Index for Singapore reservoirs using statistical and machine-learning workflows, supporting spatial comparison, temporal tracking and operational decision-making.








Developed the open-source software CoastalWQL as part of my PhD research and an R&D project with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and industry collaborator DHI. The project used drones and high-resolution hyperspectral imagery to spatially map coastal-turbidity distributions for regulatory monitoring during land-reclamation works in Tuas. https://github.com/pakhuiying/CoastalWQL
Developed image-processing and machine-learning algorithms to process, correct and georegister more than 100 GB of hyperspectral imagery, then trained a model to predict turbidity maps.
Was one of the main developers of a multispectral version of the software that led to a technology disclosure and was licensed to DHI for operational coastal-water-quality monitoring.
Received the Merit Award at the 2023 Ministry of Transport Innovations Awards for collaborative R&D on AI-enabled multispectral imaging using UAVs for turbidity monitoring.

title: Careers@Gov application guide
text:
This guide documents the application workflow observed on the Careers@Gov portal (careers.hrp.gov.sg / jobs.careers.gov.sg) while preparing an application for a Statistician role at the Department of Statistics.
The guide is intended to help populate applications accurately from the CV and approved supporting details. It does not authorise submission. Any action labelled confirmation required must be confirmed by the applicant at the time of the specific application.




Open the relevant job posting on Careers@Gov and verify the title, agency, employment type and job requirements.
Select Apply on the job posting.
Sign in or continue to the application form.
Work through the application sections shown in the wizard:

My Information
Work Experience
My Competencies
My Qualifications
Others
Attachment(s)

Save each section using its own save or save-and-close control where available.
Review the completed application. PREVIEW & SUBMIT and SUBMIT are confirmation required.




For each relevant Careers@Gov job, use the tailored-resume-generator skill before entering the application. The skill must:

analyse the full job description;
prioritise required qualifications, methods, tools, domain knowledge and repeated keywords;
map those requirements to evidence in the Word CV and the approved CV/application-details-not-in-word-cv.md file;
produce a concise, job-specific resume; and
identify gaps or details that require user input without fabricating experience.

Use the same skill workflow to prepare a tailored cover letter when the posting requests one or when a cover letter would strengthen the application. The letter should explain the fit for that specific agency and role, expand on the strongest evidence, and avoid repeating the entire resume.
Store the tailored resume and cover letter in the job’s own folder directly under CV/; do not create an additional tailored sub-folder. Save the resume in both clean DOCX and Markdown formats. Use the approved live application-details file only when a detail is relevant and labelled for reuse. Review both documents for factual accuracy before uploading.


Keep the folder name and every upload filename short enough for both Windows and employer portals. Use a conservative maximum of 60 characters for the DOCX basename, excluding the .docx extension. The full path can be longer, so keep the folder name short as well.
Use only letters, numbers, spaces and hyphens. Remove slashes, colons, ampersands, parentheses, quotation marks, en dashes, apostrophes and other symbols. Shorten the organisation to a recognised acronym or short form and shorten the job title to its core role when necessary.
Recommended pattern:
[Name]-[YYYY-MM]-[Short Job Title]-[Short Organisation].docx
Example:
Pak Hui Ying-2026-10-LTA-GIS-Analyst.docx
Use the same short basename for the Markdown source and cover letter, with a clear suffix such as -cover-letter.md. Check the character count before saving or uploading.
Do not upload the resume or cover letter automatically. Uploading either document transmits personal and professional information to the employer’s platform and requires confirmation for the specific application.

title: Cross-platform job-application workflow
text:
Do not build one brittle automation script that assumes every job platform has the same buttons or page structure. A better design is:

Keep the content layer stable: CV facts, approved work-experience descriptions, competency evidence, qualifications and reusable cover-letter themes.
Keep the interface layer platform-specific: page names, selectors, dropdown behavior, save controls and submission flow.
Require a human confirmation gate before previewing, submitting, sending, or deleting application data.

This means a reusable skill could be worthwhile later, but it should orchestrate the workflow rather than hard-code the Careers@Gov interface. A useful skill would accept the job posting, identify the platform, load the approved CV facts, draft job-specific text, flag missing information and ask for confirmation before external actions.
The tailored-resume-generator skill is the required content-generation workflow for both the tailored resume and the tailored cover letter. It should be used after the role relevance check and before the application is populated.






Record the job title, organisation, employment type and closing-date status.
Extract the role’s responsibilities, required knowledge, methods, communication expectations and teamwork expectations.
Identify which CV evidence directly supports each requirement.




For every job that passes the relevance check, create a concise, job-specific resume before beginning the application. Use the tailored-resume-generator workflow to analyse the job description, prioritise its must-have and repeated keywords, map them to substantiated CV evidence, and identify gaps without fabricating experience.
Use the Word CV as the foundation and consult CV/application-details-not-in-word-cv.md whenever an additional detail is relevant and has been approved for reuse. Details labelled VERIFY BEFORE USE, ROLE-SPECIFIC or DO NOT DISCLOSE WITHOUT APPROVAL require an explicit check before inclusion.
Create one folder per job directly under CV/; do not add a tailored sub-folder. The folder name should contain a short form of the organisation and a readable short form of the job title. Save both an upload-ready DOCX and its editable Markdown source in that folder.
Use the filename pattern:
[Name]-[YYYY-MM]-[Short Job Title]-[Short Organisation].docx
and the same basename with .md. Keep the DOCX basename to 60 characters or fewer, excluding .docx, as a conservative cross-platform limit. Keep the job folder name short too, because employer portals may impose a limit on the complete upload path rather than only the basename.
Use only letters, numbers, spaces and hyphens. Remove slashes, colons, ampersands, parentheses, quotation marks, en dashes, apostrophes and other symbols. Shorten the organisation to a recognised acronym or short form and shorten the job title to its core role when necessary. Example: Pak Hui Ying-2026-10-LTA-GIS-Analyst.docx.
Before uploading, verify the actual basename length and confirm that the file opens locally. If the portal rejects it, shorten the organisation and title further rather than changing the document contents.
Recommended content rules:

Keep the resume to two pages maximum unless the role genuinely requires more detail.
Lead with the experience, methods, tools, datasets and outcomes most relevant to the posting.
Use standard ATS-friendly headings and bullets.
Include only claims supported by the Word CV or the approved live application-details file.
Record any material gap, such as a required tool, domain or certification that is not evidenced.
Review the DOCX visually after rendering before uploading it.

Do not upload the resume automatically. Uploading a personal resume transmits personal and professional information to the employer’s platform and requires applicant confirmation for the specific application.



Use the tailored-resume-generator skill to prepare a cover letter for each relevant role when the posting requests one or when it would materially strengthen the application. The cover letter should:

address the specific organisation and job title;
connect the role’s highest-priority requirements to verified CV evidence;
use relevant details from CV/application-details-not-in-word-cv.md when their reuse label permits it;
explain transferable skills where the candidate does not have direct domain experience;
avoid unsupported claims, generic praise and repetition of the full resume; and
flag any missing motivation, availability, eligibility or job-specific information as NEEDS USER INPUT.

Save the cover letter in the same per-job folder as the tailored resume. Use a conventional, symbol-safe basename matching the job folder, with a clear suffix such as -cover-letter.md and, where needed, a DOCX version for upload. Do not upload it without applicant confirmation.



For every proposed statement, classify it as:

CV-supported — directly stated or clearly evidenced in the CV.
Previously approved detail — supplied by the applicant in the current application process.
Needs user input — cannot be safely inferred.
Do not use — unsupported, exaggerated or irrelevant.





Complete factual profile fields first.
Enter work experience using role-specific descriptions.
Add only strongly relevant competencies and use concrete evidence.
Enter qualifications and supporting items using the platform’s exact labels.
Upload only applicant-approved documents.





Confirm that entries remain visible after saving.
Check for accidental text duplication, truncation and wrong dropdown selections.
Save section-by-section if the platform supports it.





Compare the application against the job requirements.
Show the applicant any missing or uncertain fields.
Require explicit confirmation immediately before preview, send, submit or irreversible deletion.





Different platforms may use labels such as Add, Create, New, Edit, Save, Save and close, Continue, Review, Apply or Submit for equivalent actions. The agent should identify the current page’s accessible labels and confirm the meaning of an unfamiliar control before using it.
Never infer that a button is safe merely because it contains the word “save”; some portals combine saving with submission or advancement to a final review step.

Clarification: the agency engagement involved government agencies providing feedback on how the Heat Risk Index could be relevant for informing policies. Do not describe this as formal policy adoption unless separately confirmed.

Label: GENERAL REUSE for statistical, machine-learning, climate-risk, water-quality and data-science roles.
As part of my postdoctoral research on climate-risk assessment for Singapore at SMU, I used a joint-probability Bayesian model to capture dependencies between short-duration intense rainfall and total daily rainfall using historical rainfall distributions. This improved predictions of future short-duration rainfall from V3 projected total daily rainfall.
During my PhD, I published several peer-reviewed papers using machine-learning methods, including Hierarchical Bayesian Model Aggregation and XGBoost, to predict turbidity concentrations from high-dimensional hyperspectral imagery. I also trained a fully convolutional U-Net model for object segmentation in hyperspectral imagery.
During my industrial attachment with PUB’s Water Quality Department, I used machine-learning and statistical tools, including Correspondence Canonical Analysis (CCA) and exceedance anomaly detection, to investigate sources of 2-MIB and Geosmin, compounds associated with Taste and Odour (T&O) issues, and to provide insights for mitigation strategies.

Proceedings of the 39th IAHR World Congress. doi: https://10.3850/IAHR-39WC2521716X20221294.

I developed R scripts to automate the analyses.

Developed a Water Quality Index (WQI) for Singapore reservoirs to provide an optimised and efficient quantitative interpretation of reservoir water quality. The WQI supports spatial comparison across reservoirs and tracking of temporal changes in water quality. Methods from my published paper (Pak et al., 2021a) were used to develop the WQI, demonstrating its practical application and ability to operationalise quantitative water-quality assessment within the Water Quality Department. Used machine-learning and statistical tools, including Correspondence Canonical Analysis (CCA) and exceedance anomaly detection, to investigate sources of 2-MIB and Geosmin, compounds associated with Taste and Odour (T&O) issues, and to provide insights for mitigation strategies.

title: About
text:
Skills and key competencies

Geospatial analysis: Python geospatial packages including GeoPandas, Shapely, GDAL/OGR, rasterio, netCDF, and OSMnx for spatial data processing, georegistration, spatial matching, and reproducible analysis; QGIS, ArcGIS Pro, PyQGIS, and Google Earth Engine for geospatial workflows and visualisation.
Machine learning and statistical analysis: Python and R/RStudio for data wrangling, machine learning, Bayesian modelling, uncertainty and sensitivity analysis, multivariate analysis, and applied econometrics, including spatial and hedonic models.
Drone-based remote sensing: UAV multispectral and hyperspectral imagery, image correction and alignment, sun-glint correction, turbidity mapping, and processing workflows for coastal and environmental monitoring.
Water-quality modelling: Water Quality Index development, hydrology and water-quality modelling, total suspended solids retrieval, and SWAT/QSWAT/SWAT-CUP applications for riverine and reservoir systems.
Open-source tools and reproducible research: Python, R, Quarto, Git/GitHub, and open-source software development, including CoastalWQL for processing hyperspectral imagery and producing coastal-turbidity maps, and SUGAR (Sun Glint-Aware Restoration) for sun-glint correction in UAV imagery.
Field and operational practice: Water-quality sampling, stakeholder-facing decision-support tools, and a CAAS-certified Unmanned Aerial Pilot License for operating drones up to 25 kg.
